activities.caption: call the magnitude — the plant in one line of bookkeeping
activities.name: tfeTurbineEstimate

config.prompt: A large steam unit passes about 2,000 kg/s of steam, and each kilogram hands over roughly 1,100 kJ as shaft work. What electrical power does the plant make?
config.why: 1,100 kJ/kg × 2,000 kg/s = 2.2 × 10⁹ J/s ≈ 2 GW — the plant's output in one line of bookkeeping.
config.context: Every loss — bearing friction, valve throttling, stack heat — is a line item some engineer is paid to shrink.

activities.caption: pair each process with what it keeps constant
activities.name: tfeProcessMatch

config.prompt: Four named processes, four pinned properties — pair them:

pairs.right: temperature pinned — slow expansion on a heat source
no heat exchange at all — fast expansion or an insulated pipe

config.why: The names are the spec: each process pins one property, and the ideal-gas arithmetic (pv = RT, Δh = cpΔT) fills in the rest.

activities.anchor: the boiler, not the kettle, changed the world
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the boiling kettle
activities.name: tfeBoilSpot

config.prompt: This explanation of boiling contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Heating 1 kg of liquid water from freezing point to the boil costs a few hundred kilojoules.
While the liquid warms, the thermometer climbs steadily.
Boiling at atmospheric pressure absorbs about 2,257 kJ/kg.
During boiling the thermometer keeps climbing, tracking the incoming heat.
That is why steam carries far more energy per kilogram than hot water.
config.correction: During boiling the thermometer stays pinned at 100 °C — the added heat goes into the phase change, not into temperature.
config.why: Heat is energy in transit; temperature is a state variable. The phase change absorbs roughly five times the sensible heat while the thermometer holds still — steam's whole advantage.

activities.caption: put the ceiling on the scale
activities.name: tfeCarnotPlace

config.prompt: Steam at 600 °C (873 K) rejecting to a river at 30 °C (303 K): where does the maximum efficiency sit on the scale?
config.why: η = 1 − 303/873 ≈ 0.65 — a 65% ceiling fixed by the two absolute temperatures alone. Real plants reach ~45%; the gap closes only with a hotter source or a colder sink.

activities.caption: you want more work from the same fuel — pick the lever
activities.name: tfeLeverBranch

config.root: The ledger balances and the ceiling is fixed at 65%. You want more useful work from the same fuel.

start.text: Which move actually raises the ceiling?

choices.label: Better materials — supercritical steam raises T_hot
Colder cooling water — lower T_cold
choices.feedback: The second legal lever: widen the gap from below.

choices.label: Polish the machine — better bearings, tighter tolerances
choices.feedback: Helps the real engine, but the ideal is what sets the limit.

choices.label: Put the rejected heat to work instead of paying for it twice
choices.feedback: No new ceiling — but the tax bill funds a second job.

hotter.text: 1 − T_cold/T_hot rises with T_hot: this is precisely the metallurgical battle the industry actually fights.

colder.text: The ceiling rises as T_cold falls — limited only by the environment you reject into.

craft.text: The real engine creeps toward its ideal — but the ideal itself, between the same two temperatures, stops at the same 65%.

reuse.text: Cogeneration's ledger can exceed 90% because heat delivered counts too — while exergy keeps the honest score.

config.why: Only a hotter source or a colder sink moves the ceiling; isentropic polish and re-used reject heat work within it.

activities.caption: file the losses by where the work potential dies
activities.name: tfeExergyBuckets

config.prompt: An exergy audit names the big leakers — file each entropy source:

items.label: burning fuel at flame temperature against steam at steam temperature
heat flowing across a finite temperature difference in a boiler

config.why: Exergy analysis consistently names combustion and heat exchange as the big leakers — exactly where combined-cycle design aims.

config.prompt: One Rankine loop, four stations — put them in order:
items: Pump liquid water to high pressure
Boil and superheat it in the boiler
config.why: The pump handles a liquid — pumping liquid costs v·Δp and liquid volume is tiny — while the turbine handles vapour. That split is the whole trick.

activities.anchor: The fridge does not manufacture cold
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the open-door fridge
activities.name: tfeFridgePredict

config.q: On a hot day you leave the refrigerator door open, hoping to cool the kitchen. What happens to the room?
choices: It cools down — chilled air pours out
config.why: The machine pumps heat from its cabinet into the room, and the compressor's electrical work arrives as additional heat: it cools the front of the room by warming all of it slightly.
